Franz Kafka could have written a novel called The Enemy. It would have shown that what produces anxiety is the enemy’s lack of definition.
There is no other kind of anxiety. The essence of anxiety is precisely the sense that there is an enemy somewhere without knowing clearly who or what that enemy is.
Reason, by contrast—and in this sense, high politics—has the task of identifying the enemy. And identifying the enemy always means identifying oneself at the same time.
Once the enemy has been clearly defined, anxiety comes to an end. At most, fear remains.
But how are we supposed to pull anything out of this state of uncertainty and give it a definite form when we no longer possess any concepts in common?
One of the defining features of civil war is precisely that the enemies no longer share a common language of concepts. Every concept then becomes an intrusion across the enemy line.
The mistake of F. A. Kramer (Before the Ruins of Germany, Koblenz, August 1945), Reck-Malleczewen, and the others:
Such a tiny man, such an enormous sinner!

The more insignificant this Brother Straubinger is, the more remarkable the whole thing becomes. The more purely he functions as an empty amplifier, as nothing more than a device for projecting sound, the more uncanny becomes the current of power that carries him and the words that bellows so loudly.
The more he was merely a sponge soaking up some substance, the more remarkable that substance itself becomes.
And the more the explanation is reduced to individual psychology, the more it turns into self-revelation on the part of the person doing the explaining.
Eventually that self-revelation itself becomes uninteresting.
Those who destroy what is nothing destroy only themselves.
Everyone classifies himself through his enemy—through the person or thing he is willing to recognize as his enemy. That applies to Brother Straubinger.
But it applies just as much to those who declare him to be the one and only enemy and keep him alive through the idea of collective responsibility.
Now I hardly dare even draw breath, for fear of distracting the mysterious hand that is guiding things.
No comforting lie about life deceives me any longer.
The expression “life-lie,” viewed in the history of ideas, developed directly alongside the philosophy of life and was eventually drowned out by the noise of faith in life.
“The ocean is free, and freer still are springs.”
Let us see whether one springs up.
In any case, to speak today of the “freedom of the ocean” is no longer entirely honest.

In 1926 there was an attempt to draft a convention “on questions relating to the pollution of navigable waters by petroleum” (Gilbert Gidel, The Public International Law of the Sea, vol. I, 1932, p. 480). And then came the conventions for saving the whale!
So the great Leviathan itself is now under nature protection—and we are still supposed to call the ocean in which it swims a free ocean.
There can be no movement without empty space. There can also be no law without free space.
Whenever a space is brought under rules, ordered, and enclosed, there must remain another space outside it—a free space that remains outside the law.
How terrible a world would be in which there were no foreign countries left at all, only one single domestic realm.
No road leading out into the open.
No room in which free forces can measure themselves against one another and test their strength.

The religion of those who wait: waiting for the Messiah who has not yet come; waiting for the Messiah who has already come but will nevertheless come again; waiting for the Comforter and the Holy Spirit; waiting for the classless society and the eternal kingdom.
The Trinity as an expression of this waiting.
What Bruno Bauer calls Judaization is the establishment of waiting as a permanent condition: a waiting room designed to last indefinitely and made more and more comfortable as time goes on.
The traveller wants to lie down among those who are waiting and wait there for a little while.
Just as Nacht can be read as N + acht—N plus “eight”—so NORD = N + ORT.
Once again: the identity of order and location.
Metabolē, change or reversal; tropē, turning; phora, movement (Statesman, chs. 13 ff.).
“A small part of the race remains.”
“Many strange and astonishing sufferings.” That, then, is the kind of metabolē in which we are sitting today.
Understood cyclically: a world-age of reversal and counter-movement.
My impression from reading Arthur Koestler, Baumgartner’s speech, and so on:
Everything today is working toward the retroactive realization of the assumptions behind the earlier wild protests.
Indeed—today, in the most concrete form imaginable: collective guilt. These opposing camps now give one another their meaning.
Anyone who commits an injustice today can be sure that tomorrow’s injustice will provide his justification. So one anticipates these later justifications in advance.
Be bold enough to do that here too.
There is a connection between these criminalizations after the fact and these justifications after the fact.

In Hermann Hefele one finds the following pair of opposites, embedded in an entire labyrinth of antitheses that cross and recross one another thousands of times: from morality to legality —that is, from the subjectivity of individual conscience to the objectivity of the collective will.
This is then supposed to correspond to:
Today a Bavarian parliamentarian speaks of “the lack of instinct in legality.”
I reread the preface to the first volume of Sohm’s Church Law, from 1892.
Sohm appears to say quite clearly:

“Purely legal treatment has merely (!) formal value. Law does not take its content from itself. It receives that content from other powers—in the field of church law, from the religious powers of human life.”
There is something disturbing about the general, neutralizing way this is stated.
Does the entire problem simply come down to a general opposition between “mere form” and content, which is supposedly something more than mere form?
If so, then this would no longer be the painfully specific problem of church law.
And who are these “religious powers”—not merely intellectual or spiritual powers?
Does church law receive its content from a potestas spiritualis, a spiritual authority?
In short, the thorn is still there.
Francis Bacon, in Of Seditions and Troubles (chapter XV of the Sermones Fideles, 1644), warns princes against joining themselves to a political party.
His warning example is Henry III’s joining the League, which later turned against him.
The auctoritas principis, the authority of the prince, thereby becomes something secondary and dependent. There is something similar in Bodin.
I was startled by the sheer, unsupported arrogance with which Kelsen criticized my theory of the neutral guardian of the constitution and tried to discredit it as unscientific.
The essence of art also depends on form. So why can one not say: the essence of art stands in contradiction to the essence of the Church?
Does it contradict the essence of spirit that musical scores and written poems exist?
Rudolf Kassner’s comments from April 1942 in the Europäische Revue seem extraordinarily illuminating.
Hobbes is the true philosopher of the Baroque.
The Baroque puts up a façade in front of the new, Faustian world and makes that façade swell with importance. There is a separation between rule and power:
Hobbes’s separation between outside and inside, with the strongest possible emphasis on the outside, does indeed have something of this putting-forward of the façade.
“Desire of power, that ceaseth only in death.”
Even Leviathan is a mortal god, a Deus mortalis.
Kassner is entirely right when he says:

“Hobbes’s view of power is neither that of the Greek Sophists, nor that of Machiavelli, nor that of Goethe’s Mephistopheles. None of them, when thinking of power, thinks of either death or sin; they remain in the real (? sic!).”
